content: 1. The Swiss HIV Cohort Study, published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2013, examined various aspects of HIV management and outcomes. 2. Guidelines for the prevention, care, and treatment of individuals with chronic hepatitis B infection were made available by the World Health Organization, with access noted as of October 16, 2015. 3. Long-term therapy with tenofovir has been demonstrated to be effective for patients co-infected with HIV and hepatitis B virus, as reported in Gastroenterology in 2010. 4. The World Health Organization released guidelines in 2014 for the screening, care, and treatment of individuals with hepatitis C infection, with access noted as of December 9, 2015. 5. Antiretroviral-related hepatotoxicity and its clinical syndromes and consequences were discussed in Hepatology in 2010. 6. Epidemiological synergy between HIV infections and other sexually transmitted diseases was explored in a 1992 study published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 7. The role of sexually transmitted diseases in enhancing HIV transmission was confirmed in a 1998 Lancet publication, moving beyond the hypothesis stage. 8. A study in AIDS (2001) analyzed risk factors for HIV infection at both ecological and individual levels in four urban populations in sub-Saharan Africa with varying HIV prevalence. 9. A systematic review and meta-analysis in AIDS (2006) demonstrated that herpes simplex virus type 2 infection increases the risk of HIV acquisition in both men and women. 10. A nested case-control study in Rakai, Uganda, published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2003, linked HIV acquisition to genital ulcer disease and herpes simplex virus type 2 infection. 11. The association between cervical shedding of herpes simplex virus and HIV-1 was reported in AIDS (2002). 12. The frequency of symptomatic and asymptomatic herpes simplex virus type 2 reactivations among HIV-infected men was detailed in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 1998. 13. A systematic review in Sexually Transmitted Infections (2011) highlighted the prevalence of sexually transmitted co-infections in people living with HIV/AIDS and its implications for HIV treatment as prevention. 14. Human papillomavirus-associated cancers in HIV-infected individuals were discussed in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute in 2000. 15. The impact of highly active antiretroviral therapy on cervical neoplasia and cancer in HIV-infected women was reviewed in the European Journal of Cancer Prevention in 2008. 16. The incidence of cervical squamous intraepithelial lesions in HIV-infected women was reported in JAMA in 2000. 17. WHO guidelines for screening and treating precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention were accessed in October 2015. 18. Guidelines for the prevention and treatment of opportunistic infections in HIV-exposed and HIV-infected children were developed by multiple U.S. health organizations, with access noted in October 2015. 19. The British HIV Association (BHIVA) guidelines for immunization of HIV-infected adults were published in 2008. 20. A study in AIDS (2002) analyzed genotypic changes in plasma HIV-1 RNA following influenza vaccination in patients with previously undetectable viral loads. 21. HIV-1 viral load blips were found to have limited clinical significance, as reported in Antimicrobial Chemotherapy in 2006. 22. Priority interventions for HIV/AIDS prevention, treatment, and care in the health sector were outlined in a WHO document accessed in October 2015. 23. A manual on pediatric HIV care and treatment for district hospitals, including routine care for HIV-exposed and infected children, was published by WHO in 2011. 24. Trends in underlying causes of death in people with HIV from 1999 to 2011 were analyzed in a multicohort collaboration published in Lancet in 2014. 25. The epidemiology of comorbidities of HIV/AIDS and non-communicable diseases in developing countries was systematically reviewed in the Journal of Global Healthcare Systems in 2012. 26. Increased chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) among HIV-positive veterans compared to HIV-negative veterans was reported in Chest in 2006. 27. A cross-sectional study in BMC Medicine (2014) examined hypertension, kidney disease, HIV, and antiretroviral therapy among Tanzanian adults. 28. Life expectancies of South African adults starting antiretroviral treatment were analyzed in a collaborative cohort study published in PLoS Medicine in 2013. 29. Trends in cancer incidence among HIV-infected individuals and the impact of antiretroviral therapy were reported in AIDS (2009). 30. The challenges of aging with HIV in Africa were discussed in AIDS (2012). 31. Integration of HIV and non-communicable disease care in lowand middle-income countries was reviewed in Preventing Chronic Disease in 2012. 32. Leveraging HIV programs to support non-communicable disease services was discussed in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2011. 33. Coronary heart disease in HIV-infected individuals was reviewed in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2003. 34. A systematic review and meta-analysis in HIV Medicine (2012) assessed the relative risk of cardiovascular disease among people living with HIV. 35. The risk of acute myocardial infarction in HIV-infected patients was analyzed in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2015. 36. A comparison of ischemic stroke incidence in HIV-infected and non-HIV-infected patients was reported in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2012. 37. Increased rates of acute myocardial infarction and cardiovascular risk factors among HIV-infected patients were reported in the Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism in 2007. 38. The association between HIV infection and ischemic stroke incidence was analyzed in AIDS (2014). 39. The risk of acute myocardial infarction in HIV-infected individuals was reported in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2013. 40. Cardiovascular risk among adolescents perinatally infected with HIV was assessed in Circulation in 2014. 41. Cardiovascular disease in HIV patients was reviewed in Open Heart in 2015. 42. Microbial translocation as a cause of systemic immune activation in chronic HIV infection was reported in Nature Medicine in 2006. 43. The relationship between T cell activation and CD4+ T cell count in HIV-seropositive individuals with undetectable plasma HIV RNA levels was analyzed in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2008. 44. Arterial inflammation in HIV-infected patients was reported in JAMA in 2012. 45. Inflammation, coagulation, and cardiovascular disease in HIV-infected individuals were analyzed in PLoS One in 2012. 46. Protease inhibitor exposure and increased cardiovascular disease risk in HIV-infected patients were reported in HIV Medicine in 2005. 47. The association between protease inhibitor use and cardiovascular risk in HIV-infected patients was systematically reviewed in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2003. 48. Acute coronary syndromes in HIV patients were analyzed in a meta-analysis published in the European Heart Journal in 2012. 49. The risk of cardiovascular disease from antiretroviral therapy for HIV was systematically reviewed in PLoS One in 2013. 50. The class of antiretroviral drugs and the risk of myocardial infarction were analyzed in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2007. 51. The effect of cumulative exposure to abacavir on cardiovascular disease risk was studied in the Swiss HIV Cohort Study, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2015. 52. The use of nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors and the risk of myocardial infarction in HIV-infected patients was analyzed in the D:A:D study, published in Lancet in 2008. 53. Continued evidence for an association between abacavir and myocardial infarction risk was presented at the 21st Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections in 2014. 54. A meta-analysis of abacavir use and cardiovascular disease events was published in AIDS in 2011. 55. An FDA meta-analysis found no association between abacavir use and myocardial infarction, as reported in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2012. 56. CD4+ count-guided interruption of antiretroviral treatment was analyzed in the SMART study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2006. 57. Cardiovascular risk prediction in HIV-infected patients was compared using multiple models in HIV Medicine in 2016. 58. The 2013 ACC/AHA guideline on cardiovascular risk assessment was published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology in 2014. 59. The prevalence of traditional cardiovascular risk factors and evaluation of cardiovascular risk in Nigerians living with HIV was reported in the North American Journal of Medical Sciences in 2013. 60. Cardiovascular risk assessment in HIV-infected individuals in the developing world was compared using three risk equations in HIV Medicine in 2011. 61. A comparison of cardiovascular risk equations in HIV-infected individuals was published in the Scientific World Journal in 2013. 62. The cost-effectiveness of coronary artery disease screening in HIV-infected patients was analyzed in the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology in 2014. 63. Screening and assessment of coronary heart disease in HIV-infected patients were reviewed in Circulation in 2008. 64. Cardiovascular risk and its management in HIV-infected patients were discussed in Top HIV Medicine in 2007.
